..
Issued at 409 AM CDT Wed Oct 7 2026

A northwest flow pattern will persist over the Northern Plains 
through Thursday night. A surface ridge axis extends from 
western Alberta to western North Dakota early this morning, and
will remain quasi-stationary through the day today as a weak 
cold front sags into northern and eastern parts of the state. 
This will set up a breezy afternoon for the eastern half of the 
state, with slightly cooler high temperatures ranging from the 
lower and mid 60s north to lower 70s south. Surface high 
pressure is forecast to migrate southeastward tonight, with the
center of the high passing through the state during the 
nighttime hours. This would normally promote strong radiational
cooling, but confidence is high that a thicker band of 
cirrostratus clouds should mitigate cooling to some extent. The
deterministic NBM low temperature forecast for tonight is 
already cooler than the 50th percentile at most locations, so 
no deviations from that have been made. Lighter winds are 
expected on Thursday, with high temperatures mostly in the mid 
60s to lower 70s.

A potent trough digging into the Pacific Northwest on Friday 
will force a low-amplitude transient upper level ridge over the 
Northern Plains. This will allow temperatures climb around 10 
to 20 degrees above normal, with forecast highs mostly in the 
70s and lower 80s. The base of the Pacific Northwest trough is 
projected to cut off and dig deeper along the California coast 
over the weekend while the northern stream attempts to remain 
more progressive. This will push a cold front through the 
Northern Plains, with by far the coldest air mass of the season 
thus far. But there is still considerable timing uncertainty 
with the frontal passage. The GEFS tends to favor a Saturday 
afternoon/evening passage while the Canadian ensemble would 
prefer an early to mid Sunday passage. But each of those 
solutions are not exclusive to their model cores. Cluster 
analysis tends to favor a slower solution, with the front not 
arriving until after peak heating on Saturday (except perhaps 
in the far northwest). The NBM is tilted towards this solution, 
with highs on Saturday in the mid 60s northwest to around 80 in 
the southern James River Valley. Sunday will certainly be much 
colder at all locations. But outside of the northwest where 
there is high confidence in daytime maximum temperatures only 
in the 40s, the spread of the median 50 percent of the NBM 
distribution is around 10 to 15 degrees. The 25th percentile 
keeps highs in the 40s for all areas but the southern James 
River Valley, while the 75th percentile reaches the 50s 
southwest to north central, 60s south central, and even 70s in 
the southern James River Valley. The distribution spread 
decreases on Monday, with highs broadly favored in the mid 40s 
to lower 50s. The other aspect of the cool down that will need 
to be monitored is the potential for the first widespread freeze
of the season. Sunday and Monday nights are projected to be the
coldest nights, with NBM deterministic lows in the upper 20s to
mid 30s. Probabilities for sub-freezing temperatures each of 
these nights generally range from high northwest to low 
southeast. Conceptually, Monday night seems to have a better 
opportunity for below freezing temperatures with potential for 
a surface high pressure moving in, while an overcast sky is 
more likely on Sunday night.

The northern stream wave will increase precipitation chances 
across the region Sunday through Monday, but there is still 
uncertainty on location, timing, and amounts. One takeaway that
is emerging with the latest ensemble guidance is that QPF 
threshold probabilities are higher on Monday than on Sunday, as 
that is when the passage of a shortwave trough could be paired 
with a coupled jet streak. But this is not necessarily true at 
every location, and clusters depict clear uncertainty in where 
the highest QPF could fall on Monday. NBM 48-hour QPF 
probabilities (Sunday through Monday night) are highest in 
southwest North Dakota at all thresholds. But the entire 
forecast area has a 50 to 80 percent chance for at least 0.1" 
QPF, and there are medium chances for at least 0.5" QPF along 
and south and west of the Missouri River. Most of the 
precipitation will fall as rain, but temperatures both at the 
surface and aloft may be cool enough to allow snow to mix in 
Sunday night into Monday. Probabilities for measurable snow 
have increased in the NBM: now as high as 10 percent along and 
west of line from Minot to Hettinger, as well as the Turtle 
Mountains, and as high as 40 percent from around Beach to 
Bowman where there is also a 20 percent chance for exceeding 
one inch of snow. However, these snow probabilities assume a 
10:1 snow-to-liquid ratio, which is likely too high, and do not
take into account the warmer antecedent ground temperatures, 
which snowfall rates may not be high enough to overcome melting 
on contact. 

Ens
